newsitem.title: CHINA: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Chinese issuers dominate.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Chinese issuers dominate.

text.p: Chinese issuers again dominate Asian debt markets, with Taiwanese, Hong Kong and the Hong Kong branch of a European bank all expected to raise debt through U.S. or Hong Kong dollar issues.
Taiwan's Hua Nan Commercial Bank is talking to bankers about issuing US$150 million either through a floating-rate certificate of deposit (FRCD) or through a floating-rate note (FRN), bankers said.
Tenor could be for five years with pricing in the low "20s", in line with other Taiwan banks raising U.S. dollars over five years.
First Commercial Bank paid an all-in of 23 basis points last year in a five-year deal, which included a call option at year three.
Kwong On Bank is also expected to raise money through a HK$500 million FRCD.
Kwong On Bank has an A long-term rating from European agency IBCA which is high enough to qualify for the liquidity adjustment facility operated by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA).
However, the issue size would have to be doubled to HK$1 billion to meet the HKMA's liquidity requirements for the LAF.
Bankers said they had heard that Guangdong Enterprise may be looking for cash, though no further details were available.
In other news, bankers said China's new interbank market is suffering from a cash glut and a dearth of borrowers.
"There is huge money supply among banks and few need to borrow from the market," said one interbank player.
She predicted that the market would remain dull for the foreseeable future until the government set up enough mechanisms to allow more borrowers access to the system.
While the Yankee market is relatively quiet at the moment, Goldman Sachs is still working on bringing the US$400 million seven-year issue for Tjiwi Kimia to market.
Bankers said the issue's relatively long tenor reflected growing awareness of Asian credits among U.S. investors, and greater appetite for long-term debt among Asian borrowers.
Elsewhere the markets are relatively quiet after attacks on the Thai baht, the Malaysian ringgit and the Philippine peso, despite signs the peso may be stabilising.

The Philippines' central bank has cut its overnight borrowing rate to 25 percent from 28 percent, and rates of five-day, two-week and one month term reverse repos were also cut to 18 percent from 22 percent.
"As the market stabilises, we will correspondingly reduce interest rates," central bank governor Gabriel Singson said.
Thailand's finance minister, Thanong Bidaya confirmed his country is not seeking financial help from the International Monetary Fund or Japan, but did not rule it out in the future.
Thanong also said recent media reports suggesting Thailand was seeking to raise between US$10 billion and US$20 billion were groundless.
Thanong is due to meet his Japanese counterpart Takeshi Komura on Friday.

Indonesian central bank governor Sudradjad Djiwandono said widening the rupiah band had been effective in the past in dealing with inflows and outflows, but was not sure if it was enough to stem the latest turmoil.
This kind of policy step in the past hads been effective in facing income and outgoing of funds," said Djiwandono, in Tokyo for a World Bank meeting. "We don't really know whether that is enough."
